records.sourceFile: Normalization of rapid force to peak force in an isometric hamstring assessment using force plates.pdf

paper.citation: Barber R, Fahey JT, Comfort P, Ripley NJ. Normalization of rapid force to peak force in an isometric hamstring assessment using force plates. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2024;59:100450.
paper.abstract: Twenty elite female soccer players completed three maximal 90-90 isometric hamstring contractions on a force plate. Force at 100 ms and 200 ms, normalized to peak force, showed good absolute and moderate relative reliability, and the authors propose a quadrant method for combining peak force with normalized rapid force to guide training.
paper.tldr: Rapid force at 100 and 200 ms, expressed as a percentage of peak force, was measured reliably in a 90-90 isometric hamstring test on a force plate in elite female soccer players. Whether the proposed quadrant method changes training or detects fatigue is not tested here.
paper.methods: Observational reliability study of 20 elite female soccer players tested once, 72 h after a match. Each player completed three maximal isometric 90-90 hamstring trials per leg on a 1000 Hz force plate, and the mean of three trials was used. F100 and F200 were expressed as a percentage of peak force, with reliability calculated using CV% and ICC.
paper.findings: In Table 1, normalized F100 and F200 had CV 6.12-7.62% and ICC 0.689-0.721. Peak force had CV 3.05% and ICC 0.887 for the left limb and CV 2.25% and ICC 0.917 for the right limb, and no significant difference was found between limbs (P = 0.826-0.919, Hedges g 0.11-0.24). The authors describe a quadrant plot of peak force against normalized rapid force for identifying training priorities.
paper.limitations: Only one test session is described, so between-day reliability was not assessed, and the sample was a single squad of elite female players. The quadrant thresholds are the group means, and the authors state that the 90-90 position may lack specificity to the hamstring injury mechanism and that the fatigue and injury-risk applications need further research. The abstract gives ICC 0.689-0.703 for normalized rapid force, while Table 1 gives 0.689-0.721.
paper.practicalImplications: Normalized rapid force can be measured with acceptable consistency using a single-plate 90-90 test, so a practitioner could track it over time. The quadrant plot is the authors' proposal for choosing between maximal-strength and explosive-strength emphasis, and it has not been tested against training outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: In elite female soccer players, rapid force at 100 and 200 ms normalized to peak force was reproducibly measured in a 90-90 hamstring test on a force plate. The authors propose using peak force and normalized rapid force together to choose between maximal-strength and explosive-strength work, but this use is untested.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only uninjured players, and the normalized measures have not been shown to track recovery, readiness or re-injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Objective measures of strain and subjective muscle soreness differ between positional groups and season phases in American college football.pdf

paper.citation: McKay BA, Delaney JA, Simpkin A, Larkin T, Murray A, Daniels D, et al. Objective Measures of Strain and Subjective Muscle Soreness Differ Between Positional Groups and Season Phases in American College Football. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. Ahead of print, 2023.
paper.abstract: Repeated-measures study of 23 male American college football players across off-season, fall camp and in-season phases, comparing oxidative stress markers, countermovement jump variables and subjective muscle soreness by position group. In 'Bigs' (offensive and defensive linemen), redox markers, jump variables and soreness were higher in the off-season than in the other phases, and 'Skills' showed no significant phase differences in redox markers.
paper.tldr: In one college football team, linemen ('Bigs') showed the highest oxidative strain and soreness in the off-season, a phase where their share of high-speed running was descriptively higher. Position groups should be reviewed separately rather than as one squad.
paper.methods: Weekly point-of-care capillary blood tests (FORT, FORD and derived OSI), countermovement jumps on force plates and a subjective soreness questionnaire were collected over 10 weeks. Linear mixed models with athlete as a random effect compared phases and position groups. GPS data were described but not included in the statistical analysis because about 25% was missing.
paper.findings: In the off-season, FORT, FORD, OSI and soreness were higher in 'Bigs' than in fall camp and in-season, and their jump flight time and RSImod were also highest then (for soreness, the in-season value was also higher than fall camp). 'Combos' showed lower FORT and OSI in the off-season than in the later phases. Between groups, FORT was higher in 'Bigs' than 'Combos' in all three phases, OSI was higher in 'Bigs' than 'Combos' and 'Skills' in the off-season, and FORD was higher in 'Skills' than 'Bigs' in the off-season. The authors report that 'Skills' showed no significant phase differences in FORT, FORD or OSI.
paper.limitations: The study covers one team of 23 players, with 3 off-season and 3 in-season weeks of data, so it does not capture a full season. GPS data were about 25% missing and were not statistically tested. The authors note that CMJ has not been validated as a fatigue measure in American football and that the wellness questionnaire is not formally validated.
paper.practicalImplications: Analyze position groups separately when reviewing team strain data, because the groups differed in redox markers and soreness within the same phase. The authors suggest individual adaptive ranges across season phases to identify maladaptation. They also suggest that rising FORT or FORD with falling CMJ performance may indicate detrimental fatigue, though this was not tested against outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Review FORT/FORD, CMJ and soreness by position group and season phase, using each athlete's own history rather than one team norm. In this team the largest strain signal for linemen coincided with off-season conditioning, so staff can check off-season running load for that group first, though the study did not test load as a cause.
paper.rtp: The players were tracked during training and competition, and the paper does not assess injured players or return to play. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: On-field kinematics of cut maneuvers in football players - Are wearable sensors reliable for assessing anterior cruciate ligament injury risk.pdf

paper.citation: Di Paolo S, Gokeler A, Benjaminse A, Zaffagnini S, Bragonzoni L. On-field kinematics of cut maneuvers in football players: Are wearable sensors reliable for assessing anterior cruciate ligament injury risk? Journal of Sports Sciences. 2025.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of youth academy soccer players (47 enrolled: 27 male, 20 female) performing a planned Agility T-test and an unplanned football-specific cut, measured with eight wearable inertial sensors. It reports test-retest and side-to-side reliability of joint kinematics and normative values by sex, for use in ACL injury prevention work.
paper.tldr: Wearable inertial sensors gave moderate-to-excellent test-retest reliability for most joint measures during on-field cutting, with weaker side-to-side reliability. Female youth players cut with different knee and trunk patterns than males, but the study does not show that these patterns predict ACL injury.
paper.methods: Players performed two trials per side of a planned 90-degree Agility T-test and an unplanned deceiving cut on artificial turf, with eight MTw Awinda sensors recording at 100 Hz. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1), root mean square error and pooled T-scores assessed test-retest and side-to-side reliability. Male and female values were compared with t-tests or Mann-Whitney tests and Cohen's d. The sample size was estimated a priori at 44 players.
paper.findings: Test-retest reliability was moderate to excellent for most parameters (r = 0.40 to 0.92 in the Agility T-test), while side-to-side reliability was poorer, with excellent values mainly for pelvis and trunk flexion. Sagittal-plane measures were the most reliable, and the authors judged pelvis and trunk frontal-plane values not sufficiently reliable. In the Agility T-test, females had lower knee, pelvis and trunk flexion at peak knee flexion (d = 0.50 to 0.58) and greater frontal-plane range of motion at knee, pelvis and trunk (d = 0.57 to 0.59, from the text); in the deceiving cut, females had lower knee flexion (d = 0.39) and lower trunk lateral tilt (d = 0.73). Females also had lower approach velocity and lower high-intensity acceleration and deceleration percentages (d up to 1.53).
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so day-to-day reliability and change over time were not measured. Only one sensor type was used, the deceiving cut could not be standardized for speed or angle, and all players were healthy youth, so the findings may not apply to adults or injured players. The text reports four excluded players while Table 1 lists 47. Several sex differences cited in the text (peak knee external rotation d = 1.1, frontal ROM) are in appendices not in the main table, and for the deceiving cut the text reports greater female knee internal rotation while Table 3 shows more external rotation at peak knee flexion (-2.2 vs -0.7 degrees).
paper.practicalImplications: Check the reliability of each joint measure before using wearable data for an individual player, and treat side-to-side differences and pelvis or trunk frontal-plane values with caution. Use sex-specific values as reference points rather than injury-risk cut-offs. The authors advise against judging ACL risk from single peak values and suggest multi-plane analysis of whole-movement patterns.
paper.athleteDev: For academy testing, rely more on sagittal-plane knee and hip measures from wearables than on frontal or transverse-plane values, which the study found less reliable. Compare players with sex-specific reference values, and where possible test cutting in game-like conditions, as the authors recommend.
paper.rtp: The study included healthy youth players only and did not compare injured or post-surgical players. It cannot be used to make return-to-sport decisions, although the authors suggest future studies in cleared ACL-injured players.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing MRI annotation workflows for high-accuracy deep learning thigh muscle segmentation in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Slutsky-Ganesh AB, Baup S, Bharadwaj UU, Slaton JA, Valencia M, Diekfuss JA, et al. Optimizing MRI annotation workflows for high-accuracy deep learning thigh muscle segmentation in athletes. Radiology Advances. 2026;3(1):umag005.
paper.abstract: Thigh muscle MRI from 94 male professional football athletes and 67 athletes with acute ACL injury was used to train nnU-Net deep learning models on 5 to 120 annotated subjects, tested on a fixed set of 41 subjects. Twenty training subjects reached a mean Dice of 0.94 against assisted manual segmentation, and fat fraction and diffusion measures agreed closely with manual values.
paper.tldr: In single-site 3 T MRI of football and ACL-injured athletes, a deep learning model trained on 20 annotated thigh scans reached a Dice of 0.94 against assisted manual masks on 41 held-out scans. Agreement was measured against the same semi-automatic ground truth, so the model is not yet validated on other scanners or populations.
paper.methods: Fourteen thigh muscles were segmented on IDEAL water images with semi-automatic 3D propagation followed by manual correction, and these assisted manual masks served as ground truth. nnU-Net models were trained on 13 training-set sizes from 5 to 120 subjects and evaluated on a fixed test set of 41 subjects (34 athletes, 7 ACL). Accuracy was assessed with Dice, relative volume difference, Hausdorff distance, HD95 and average symmetric surface distance, and fat fraction and DTI values from automatic and manual masks were compared by ICC and Bland-Altman analysis.
paper.findings: At 20 training subjects the grand-total results were Dice 0.94 ± 0.02, relative volume difference 4.9% ± 5.2%, ASSD 0.8 ± 0.4 mm and HD95 3.2 ± 2.0 mm, meeting the authors' a priori reliability thresholds. The authors report that 50 subjects first met the stricter thresholds (Table 1: Dice 0.95 ± 0.02, RVD 3.5%, ASSD 0.7 mm, HD95 2.8 mm), and 120 subjects gave Dice 0.95 ± 0.02. Volume ICC was 0.995 and fat fraction ICC was 0.989 at 20 subjects, and the open-source MuscleMap model scored a Dice of 0.65 ± 0.21 on the same test set.
paper.limitations: All data came from one site on a single 3 T GE system, and the cohort was largely male and young (the ACL group had a mean age of 17.0 years, with 23 of 67 male), so generalization to other scanners, protocols and populations is untested; five of 41 test subjects were also excluded from DTI analyses. Agreement is measured against assisted manual masks rather than an independent gold standard, and the 20-subject operating point was identified from learning curves computed on the same fixed test set used to report accuracy. Text and tables conflict: the abstract gives HD95 as 3.2 ± 2.8 mm against 3.2 ± 2.0 mm in Table 1, and the Results say Dice was 'consistently >0.95 with Ntrain = 30 or more' while Table 1 shows 0.95 ± 0.02 at 50 and 120, so table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Labs with a similar 3 T IDEAL and DTI protocol could build a site-specific model from roughly 20 carefully annotated scans, which reached the authors' reliability thresholds on held-out data. Local validation against manual masks is still needed before the outputs are used for athlete decisions, and the released model is licensed for research use only (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
paper.athleteDev: Automated thigh segmentation with fat fraction and diffusion outputs could support repeated measurement of muscle size and composition in athletes, with less manual annotation time. The paper tests segmentation accuracy and biomarker agreement only, not whether these measures detect changes in performance, so it supports a measurement method rather than a training decision.
paper.rtp: The study supports quantitative muscle MRI as a measurement method in ACL-injured athletes, but the ACL group was used only for segmentation accuracy and not for recovery outcomes. It cannot show that these measures track rehabilitation or inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Performance and symmetry measures during vertical jump testing at return to sport after ACL reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Kotsifaki R, Sideris V, King E, Bahr R, Whiteley R. Performance and symmetry measures during vertical jump testing at return to sport after ACL reconstruction. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study used dual force plates to test vertical jumps in athletes at return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and in healthy professional football players. Athletes after ACLR remained asymmetrical in the concentric phase and during landing from bilateral jumps, and most performance metrics were still lower than in controls. Normative jump data for professional football players are also reported.
paper.tldr: Athletes cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction still showed concentric and landing asymmetries in vertical jumps, and most jump performance metrics had not returned to control values. Vertical jump testing, especially single-leg drop jump metrics, may help identify deficits that standard discharge criteria do not show.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional comparison of 126 male professional or recreational athletes after ACLR, tested within 2 weeks of clearance to return to sport, with 532 male professional soccer players as controls. Four jumps (countermovement, single-leg countermovement, double-leg drop jump and single-leg drop jump) were analysed with ForceDecks software, and between-group differences were tested using mixed-effects models; performance metrics were compared only between professional ACLR athletes and controls.
paper.findings: Concentric impulse symmetry was lower after ACLR in all four jumps (P < 0.001). Peak landing force asymmetry was greater than in controls for the countermovement jump (mean difference -11.6 percentage points, 95% CI -15.4 to -7.9) and the double-leg drop jump (-8.9, 95% CI -14.9 to -2.8), and eccentric impulse asymmetry was greater in the single-leg drop jump only (-3.8, 95% CI -5.8 to -1.7, P = 0.018). Among professional athletes, jump height after ACLR was below controls in the countermovement jump (33.3 vs 36.3 cm) and in the single-leg jumps, and the single-leg drop jump showed the most residual deficits.
paper.limitations: The study used a single-institution, male-only sample, the ACLR group is mostly professional (94 of 126) and its sport is not reported. Sample sizes differ by test, and the controls differ in activity level, so the comparisons are not matched. The Discussion states there were no eccentric deceleration impulse differences at return to sport, but the abstract and Table 2 report a significant eccentric impulse difference in the single-leg drop jump (P = 0.018); this summary follows Table 2, and Table 3 also reports a recreational drop-jump height of 27.3 ± 56.7, which looks like a typographical error.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that vertical jumps, including single- and double-leg tests, should be part of periodic and return-to-sport testing after ACLR. Clinicians should track jump height, reactive strength index and contact time as well as symmetry, and plyometric training should be part of rehabilitation because single-leg drop jump deficits remained. These suggestions follow from the residual asymmetries observed, but the study does not show that addressing them lowers re-injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: The study gives normative vertical jump values for professional football players, such as a countermovement jump height of 36.3 ± 5.4 cm (Table 3), which performance staff can use as reference points. It shows that concentric impulse and reactive strength index remained lower after ACLR, so these metrics are worth tracking in return-to-performance testing.
paper.rtp: The study informs return-to-sport testing: athletes cleared under standard criteria (including quadriceps and hop limb symmetry above 90%) still showed jump asymmetries at about 9 months after surgery. It cannot show that these deficits predict re-injury or that jump tests should decide clearance, because no injury outcomes were followed.

records.sourceFile: Performing Nordic hamstring strength testing with additional weight affects the maximal eccentric force measured - Do not compare apples to oranges.pdf

paper.citation: Amundsen R, Møller M, Bahr R. Performing Nordic hamstring strength testing with additional weight affects the maximal eccentric force measured: do not compare apples to oranges. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023;9:e001699.
paper.abstract: In 140 football players (84 women, 56 men), maximal eccentric hamstring force measured on a Nordic device rose when 5 kg or 10 kg of added weight was used, compared with no added weight. The rise occurred in players who could and could not control the final phase, so that criterion should not decide whether weight is used.
paper.tldr: Adding weight to the Nordic hamstring test raises the force measured, whether or not the athlete can control the final phase. Use the same test load for pre and post testing, and do not use the control criterion to choose load.
paper.methods: Female (n=84) and male (n=56) football players performed three maximal Nordic test sets with 0, 5 and 10 kg vests, and 10 men were also tested at 15 and 20 kg. Control of the final phase (about the last 20 degrees) was judged by visual inspection, and differences were analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA and independent t-tests.
paper.findings: Maximal force was higher with 5 kg (women +8 N, 2%; men +18 N, 4%) and 10 kg (women +17 N, 5%; men +27 N, 6%) than with no added weight, in players who could (n=65) and could not (n=75) control the final phase. For men, the extra rise with 10 kg was larger in players who could control the phase (17 N, p=0.004), but this difference was not seen in women.
paper.limitations: Control of the final phase was judged by visual inspection, and its reliability was not tested. Loads were always applied in the same increasing order (0, 5, then 10 kg), so order effects such as learning cannot be ruled out, and the 15 and 20 kg analysis includes only 10 men with low power and unadjusted multiple comparisons. Women and men were tested in different squads and seasons (2021 and 2022), so sex and test season cannot be separated.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the same added weight for pre and post Nordic testing, or test all players with the same load, and do not choose load by whether the athlete can control the final phase. If weight is used, increase it until force plateaus, as the authors recommend.
paper.athleteDev: Keep the Nordic test protocol, including any added load, identical across pre and post testing so that changes are not produced by the protocol. The 2 to 8% rise with load is similar to the test's measurement error, so changes in individual athletes need care when interpreted.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport, injury risk or hamstring rehabilitation criteria. Its load-consistency point may help if the same test tracks strength during rehabilitation, but it sets no return-to-play threshold.
